intro: A jar of milkweed leaves sits by a classroom window. In a month, five tiny eggs become five orange butterflies that fly off toward Mexico. Near Braidwood, a hammer taps a rust-colored rock, and it splits open on an animal that has been dead for 300 million years. Both are stories about life: how it begins, how it grows, how it passes on its traits, and how it ends.

Follow the life cycles of frogs, butterflies, beans and oaks. Find out why you look like your parents but not exactly like your brother or sister. See how a heart, a root, an eye and a shell each do a job that keeps a living thing alive. Then watch what happens when a pond dries up or a prairie becomes a farm.

By the end, you will be able to explain what a trait is and where it comes from, how a structure helps a plant or animal survive, how your senses reach your brain, and what a fossil in an Illinois rock can tell us about a world that is gone.
bigQuestion: How do living things grow, pass on their traits and survive in a changing world?

timeline.t: Robert Hooke looks at thin slices of cork through a microscope and names the tiny boxes he sees 'cells'
Nicolas Steno argues that rock layers pile up over time and that fossils are the remains of once-living things
Maria Sibylla Merian publishes her paintings of caterpillars, chrysalises and the butterflies they become
Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, explaining how helpful traits spread over generations
Gregor Mendel reports his pea-plant experiments showing that traits pass to offspring in predictable patterns
The last passenger pigeon, once among the most common birds in North America, dies in a zoo; the kind is extinct
Francis Tully splits open a Mazon Creek concretion near Braidwood and finds the first Tully monster
Field Museum scientist Eugene Richardson names the fossil Tullimonstrum
Illinois names the monarch its state insect; the same year, the monarchs' winter home in Mexico's mountains is found
The Tully monster becomes the Illinois state fossil
Bison return to the Illinois prairie at Nachusa Grasslands, more than 150 years after they were gone from the state

test.q: Which stage comes right after the caterpillar stage in a monarch's life cycle?
test.why: The order is egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult. A tadpole is a young frog, not a butterfly.

test.q: A tadpole breathes with gills. An adult frog breathes with lungs. What is the big change between them called?
test.why: Metamorphosis is the change of body form from a young animal to an adult.

choices: A dog's weight after a big meal
test.why: Fur color is passed from parents. A scar, a trick and a full belly come from things that happen during life.

test.q: Two bean plants from the same pod look different after a week in different places. The best explanation is:
test.why: Seeds from one pod share parents. Light, water and other parts of the environment changed how they grew.

test.q: Why is variation among brothers and sisters expected?
choices: They are born in different years
Each gets its own mix of traits from both parents
Only one of them inherits traits
test.why: Each child gets traits from both parents, and the mix is a little different every time.

test.q: A woodpecker with a stronger beak finds more food in winter. Over many generations, what would you predict?
test.why: Birds with the advantage survive and have young, and the young often inherit the stronger beak.

test.q: Why are many male birds brightly colored?
choices: Bright colors hide them from hawks
Females tend to choose bright males, so the trait is passed on
test.why: Bright males win more mates and have more young. That is sexual selection.

test.q: Which structure helps a plant take in water?
test.why: Roots reach into the soil and take in water. Petals attract insects, thorns defend, and leaves catch light.

choices: Turns light into signals for the brain
test.why: The retina is the layer at the back of the eye packed with cells that change light into signals.

test.q: A loud bang makes you jump. Which came first?
choices: Your ears sent a signal to your brain
test.why: The sense comes first. Ears send the signal along nerves, the brain decides, and then the muscles move.

test.q: Which is a benefit of living in a group?
test.why: More eyes mean danger is spotted sooner. Food still has to be shared, and sickness can spread faster.

test.q: A river floods a field for a whole summer. What can happen to the animals there?
choices: Some survive, some move, some die
test.why: When the environment changes, the result depends on each animal's traits: survive, move or die.

test.q: What is needed for a dead animal to become a fossil?
choices: It must be buried quickly in mud or sand
test.why: Quick burial keeps scavengers and oxygen away, so the remains last long enough to turn to stone.

test.q: Fossil corals are found across Illinois. Scientists infer that:
choices: Illinois was once under a shallow sea
test.why: Corals live in the sea. Their fossils in Illinois rock show a sea once covered the state.

test.q: The Tully monster is extinct. What does that mean?
choices: It only comes out at night
test.why: Extinct means no living members of that kind are left anywhere on Earth.

write.prompt: Choose one living thing from this unit: a monarch, a frog, an oak, a heron, or the Tully monster. Make a claim about one of its structures or traits and how it helps the living thing survive, grow or reproduce. Support your claim with evidence from the lessons and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the structure or trait and say what job it does, in one sentence.
Evidence: use at least two facts from the readings, the data tables or the fossil story.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence shows the structure helps with survival, growth or reproduction.
The other side: describe one way the same structure could be a cost, and explain why the benefit still wins.

title: Life: Cycles, Traits and Survival

chapters.title: Life Cycles and Traits
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do living things look like their parents, but never exactly the same?

story.title: The Monarchs of Room 12
story.kicker: A jar of milkweed leaves, five tiny eggs, and a class that learned to wait.
paragraphs: In September, Ms. Ortiz brought a jar of milkweed leaves into Room 12. On the bottom of one leaf were five eggs. Each egg was smaller than the head of a pin. It was pale yellow and shaped like a tiny football. The class put the jar by the window and started a chart. Day 1: five eggs. Nothing else to report.

On Day 4, a student named Jamal shouted. One egg had a hole in it. A caterpillar the size of a grain of rice was chewing its way out. Then it did something strange. It ate its own eggshell. Over the next two weeks, the caterpillars ate and ate. They grew striped in yellow, black and white. Each one shed its skin four times, like a jacket that got too tight.

On Day 18, the biggest caterpillar climbed to the lid of the jar. It hung upside down in the shape of the letter J. The next morning it was gone. In its place hung a smooth green case with gold dots. It looked like a jewel. The class called it a chrysalis. For ten days it did not seem to move at all. Some students thought it had died.

On Day 29, the green case turned dark. Then it turned clear. Through the shell the class could see orange and black wings folded up tight. At 10:15 that morning the shell split. A wet, crumpled butterfly crawled out. It hung still while its wings filled out and dried. By lunch, it was a monarch, the state insect of Illinois.

Two of the five butterflies had a small black spot on each back wing. Ms. Ortiz explained that those two were males. All five had the same orange and black pattern as their parents, who the class had never seen. But no two were exactly the same size. On a sunny afternoon the class let them go in the school garden. It was late September. Those monarchs were about to fly roughly 2,000 miles to the mountains of Mexico.
story.think: The class never saw the parents of these butterflies. How could they still know what the parents looked like?

lessons.title: The Same Four Stages
lessons.mainIdea: Every living thing is born, grows, may reproduce, and dies, and the cycle starts again with the next generation.
reading: A puppy is born. It grows into a dog. That dog may have puppies of its own. Someday the dog dies. Its puppies grow up and have puppies. This pattern is called a *life cycle*. Every kind of living thing has one. A sunflower has one. A frog has one. So do you.

All life cycles share the same big stages. First comes birth, which for many living things means hatching or sprouting. Then comes growth. Next, an adult may *reproduce*, which means making new living things like itself. Last comes death. The cycle does not end there, because the young ones carry it on.

The stages are the same, but the details are wildly different. A mayfly may live as an adult for only a day. A bur oak can stand for 300 years. Some animals are born looking like tiny adults. Others, like frogs, change shape completely. Scientists compare life cycles to find what all living things have in common.

words.d: the stages a living thing goes through: birth, growth, reproduction and death
to make new living things of the same kind

look.title: The Class Pet's Story
look.text: Room 12 also has a class hamster named Biscuit. Biscuit was born in a pet store in the spring. She is now full grown and about the size of a tennis ball. Hamsters usually live about two to three years. Some hamsters have a litter of six or more babies.
look.prompt: Which stages of the life cycle has Biscuit already gone through? Which have not happened yet?

check.q: What do all life cycles have in common?
check.why: Every living thing is born, grows, may reproduce and dies. Hatching, changing shape and long life happen only for some kinds.

check.q: A mayfly and a bur oak both have life cycles. Which sentence is true?
choices: Only the oak really has a life cycle
Both have the same stages, but the stages last very different times
Both live about the same number of years
The mayfly skips the growth stage
check.why: Both go through birth, growth, reproduction and death. A mayfly adult may live a day; an oak may live 300 years.

check.q: Why does a life cycle not end when one animal dies?
choices: Because its young carry on the cycle
Because the cycle only has three stages
check.why: The animal's offspring are born, grow and reproduce, so the cycle continues with the next generation.

lessons.title: A Frog Changes Shape
lessons.mainIdea: A frog starts as an egg in water, lives as a tadpole with gills and a tail, and slowly changes into an air-breathing adult.
reading: In April, an Illinois pond is full of frog eggs. Each egg is a black dot inside a ball of clear jelly. The eggs float in clumps near the shore. After one to three weeks, tiny *tadpoles* wiggle out. A tadpole does not look like a frog at all. It has a round body, a long tail and no legs. It breathes water through *gills*, like a fish.

The tadpole eats and grows. Then the changes begin. Two back legs sprout. Then two front legs appear. Lungs grow inside its body. The tail gets shorter and shorter. It is not cut off. The body slowly takes the tail back in and uses it as food. Finally, a small frog with no tail hops onto the shore and breathes air.

This big change in body shape is called *metamorphosis*. The word means change of form. How long it takes depends on the kind of frog. A spring peeper can finish in a couple of months. A bullfrog tadpole may stay in the water through a whole winter. The adult frog lays eggs in the pond, and the cycle starts again.

words.d: the young stage of a frog, which lives in water and has a tail and gills
body parts that take oxygen out of water, used by fish and tadpoles
a big change in body shape as a young animal becomes an adult

look.title: Two Photos From the Pond
look.text: Look at two pictures taken at the same pond. In the first, from May, the shallow water is crowded with black tadpoles the size of jelly beans. In the second, from August, there are no tadpoles. Small frogs sit along the muddy edge, and a few still have a stub of a tail.
look.prompt: What happened between May and August? What does the stub of a tail tell you?

check.q: How does a tadpole breathe?
choices: With lungs, like an adult frog
It does not need to breathe
check.why: A tadpole lives in water and takes oxygen from the water with gills. Lungs grow later, during metamorphosis.

check.q: What happens to a tadpole's tail?
choices: It falls off in one piece
The body slowly takes it back in
It grows into the back legs
It stays on the adult frog
check.why: The tail is not cut off. The body slowly absorbs it and uses it as food while the frog finishes changing.

check.q: Which change would you expect to see FIRST as a tadpole becomes a frog?
check.why: The back legs appear first. The front legs come next, the tail shrinks, and only then does the frog leave the water.

lessons.title: A Butterfly's Four Stages
lessons.mainIdea: A monarch passes through four stages, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult, and each stage has a different job.
reading: A monarch has four stages. It starts as an egg the size of a pinhead. A female lays each egg on a *milkweed* leaf. Only milkweed will do, because monarch caterpillars eat nothing else. In about four days, a caterpillar chews its way out. The caterpillar's job is simple: eat. In about two weeks it grows roughly 2,000 times heavier than when it hatched.

Next the caterpillar hangs upside down and sheds its skin one last time. Underneath is a smooth green case called a *chrysalis*. Inside, the insect's body is being rebuilt. Wings, long legs and a coiled drinking tube take shape. Nothing seems to happen on the outside. Inside, almost everything is changing.

After about ten days, the case splits and an adult butterfly climbs out. The adult's job is different from the caterpillar's job. It drinks *nectar* from flowers, finds a mate and lays eggs. It cannot chew leaves at all. Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult: this is one full turn of the monarch's life cycle.

words.d: a wild plant with milky sap; the only food monarch caterpillars eat
the hard case a caterpillar forms while it changes into a butterfly
the sweet liquid inside flowers that butterflies and bees drink

look.title: How Long Each Monarch Stage Lasts
look.cite: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service monarch pages, rounded
look.prompt: About how many days pass from egg to adult? Which stage is longest?

check.q: Where does a monarch lay her eggs?
check.why: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, so the female lays each egg on a milkweed leaf.

check.q: What is happening inside the chrysalis?
choices: The insect is resting and nothing changes
The caterpillar is eating stored leaves
The body is being rebuilt into a butterfly
check.why: The outside looks still, but inside the body is being rebuilt with wings, long legs and a drinking tube.

check.q: Using the data, about how many days does it take to go from egg to adult butterfly?
check.why: Add the egg, caterpillar and chrysalis stages: 4 + 12 + 10 = 26 days, about four weeks.

lessons.title: A Bean and an Oak
lessons.mainIdea: Plants have life cycles too: a seed sprouts, grows, makes flowers and seeds, and dies, quickly for a bean and slowly for an oak.
reading: Put a bean seed in a wet paper towel. In two or three days the seed swells and splits. A white root pokes out and heads down. A pale shoot heads up. This is *germination*, the sprouting of a seed. The seed's food is stored inside it, so the plant can grow before it has leaves.

A bean plant grows fast. In a few weeks it has leaves and flowers. Each flower turns into a pod. Inside the pod are new bean seeds. By fall, the bean plant dies. The whole cycle takes one summer. But its seeds can wait in the soil and sprout next spring.

An oak starts the same way, from a seed called an *acorn*. But an oak does not hurry. It may grow 20 years or more before it makes its first acorns. A white oak, the state tree of Illinois, can live for several hundred years. Same stages: seed, *seedling*, adult, seeds. Very different clock.

words.d: the sprouting of a seed, when the root and shoot first grow out
the seed of an oak tree
a young plant that has just sprouted from a seed

look.title: The Bean Journal
look.text: Day 1: seed is hard and white. Day 3: seed is fat and the coat is split; a root 1 cm long. Day 5: root 4 cm, shoot bent like a hook. Day 7: shoot straight, two leaves open, green. Day 14: plant 15 cm tall, four leaves.
look.prompt: What grew first, the root or the shoot? Why might that be useful for the plant?

check.q: What comes out of a bean seed first?
check.why: The root comes out first and heads down to find water. The shoot and leaves follow.

check.q: How is an oak's life cycle different from a bean's?
choices: An oak does not make seeds
An oak takes many years for each stage; a bean takes one summer
A bean lives longer than an oak
check.why: Both have the same stages, but a bean finishes in one summer while an oak may take 20 years just to make its first acorns.

check.q: Where does a sprouting bean get food before it has leaves?
choices: From food stored inside the seed
check.why: Food is stored inside the seed. That is why a bean can sprout on a paper towel with no soil.

lessons.title: What a Trait Is
lessons.mainIdea: A trait is a feature of a living thing, and many traits are inherited, passed from parents to their young.
reading: Look at your hand. Your fingers, your skin color, the shape of your thumbnail: each is a *trait*. A trait is a feature a living thing has. Eye color is a trait. A cat's stripes are a trait. A pea plant's flower color is a trait. Traits can be seen, or measured, or both.

Many traits are *inherited*. That means they are passed from parents to *offspring*. A calico cat's kittens are often calico. Two tall parents usually have tall children. Monarchs are orange and black because their parents were. The instructions for these traits are inside every living thing, and a copy goes to each of the young.

Farmers have known about inherited traits for thousands of years. They saved seeds from the sweetest corn. They bred the cows that gave the most milk. In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel counted thousands of pea plants. He showed that traits pass from parents to offspring in patterns you can predict.

words.d: a feature of a living thing, such as eye color or leaf shape
passed from parents to their young
the young of a living thing; its children

look.title: Mendel Counts His Peas
look.text: In his 1866 paper, Mendel explained that he had grown and counted pea plants for eight years. He crossed plants with round seeds and plants with wrinkled seeds. He reported that the first generation all had round seeds, and that in the next generation about three plants in four had round seeds and one in four had wrinkled seeds.
look.cite: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybrids, 1866 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why did Mendel count so many plants instead of just a few?

check.q: Which of these is an inherited trait?
check.why: Eye color is passed from parents. A scar, a language and a favorite song all come from what happens during your life.

check.q: What does 'inherited' mean?
check.why: An inherited trait comes from the parents. It is not learned, chosen or caused by the weather.

check.q: Mendel crossed round-seed peas with wrinkled-seed peas. In the first generation, what did he see?
check.why: The first generation all had round seeds. Wrinkled seeds showed up again only in the next generation, about one in four.

lessons.title: Why Brothers and Sisters Differ
lessons.mainIdea: Offspring get traits from both parents, so brothers and sisters are alike in many ways but never exactly the same.
reading: A litter of puppies is born. Same mother, same father, same day. Yet one puppy is brown, one is black, and one has a white paw. One grows bigger than the rest. This is *variation*. It means members of a family, or of a kind, are different from one another.

Variation happens because each young one gets traits from both parents. The mix is a little different every time. One puppy may get its mother's ears and its father's color. Another may get the reverse. Only *identical* twins start with the same instructions. Even they can end up a bit different.

Variation is easy to see if you look closely. Pick up ten acorns from one white oak. Measure them. Some are long, some are round, some have thick caps. Look at monarchs from the same egg batch. Some have wider black lines. Charles Darwin noticed that no two members of a kind are ever exactly alike. That idea became one of the most important in all of science.

words.d: the differences among members of one family or one kind of living thing
exactly the same

look.title: Darwin's Last Sentence
look.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859 (last sentence of the first edition)
look.prompt: Darwin says forms of life 'are being' made, not just 'have been.' What do you think he means?

check.q: Puppies in one litter have different colors. What is this called?
check.why: Variation means the members of a family or kind differ from one another, even with the same parents.

check.q: Why are brothers and sisters not exactly the same?
choices: Each gets a different mix of traits from both parents
Only the oldest child inherits traits
Traits are picked at random from strangers
check.why: Each child gets traits from both parents, but the mix is a little different every time.

check.q: You measure ten acorns from one tree. What would you predict?
choices: All ten are exactly the same size
They are all different kinds of seed
Most will be similar, but none will be exactly alike
check.why: Acorns from one tree share many traits, but variation means no two are exactly the same.

lessons.title: The World Shapes Traits Too
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits are changed by the environment, by food, sunlight, weather and experience, not only by what parents pass on.
reading: Grow two bean plants from seeds off the same pod. Put one in a sunny window. Put the other in a dark closet. In a week, the sunny plant is short, green and sturdy. The closet plant is tall, thin and yellow-white. Same parents, same instructions, very different plants. The difference came from the *environment*, everything around the plant.

Animals are shaped by their environment too. A well-fed dog grows bigger than its hungry brother. A flamingo is pink only if it eats pink shrimp and algae. Without them, its feathers turn pale. Your skin gets darker in summer sun. Muscles grow when you use them. A scar comes from a cut. None of these were passed on by parents. They are *acquired traits*, picked up during life.

Some traits come from both. Height is inherited, but a child with poor food may not reach it. The language you speak is not inherited at all. You learned it from the people around you. Scientists ask a careful question about every trait: how much comes from the parents, and how much from the world?

words.d: everything around a living thing: light, water, food, weather and other living things
a feature a living thing gets from its surroundings or experience, not from its parents

look.title: Hydrangeas on Two Sides of the Street
look.text: On Maple Street, two neighbors planted cuttings from the same hydrangea bush. Cuttings are pieces of one plant, so they carry the same instructions. One yard has sour, acid soil. Its flowers came out blue. The other yard has sweeter, chalky soil. Its flowers came out pink.
look.prompt: The plants have the same instructions. Why are the flowers different colors? Is flower color inherited, acquired, or both?

check.q: Two bean plants from the same pod grow differently in sun and in a closet. What caused the difference?
check.why: The seeds came from the same pod and are the same age. Light, part of the environment, made the difference.

check.q: Which trait is acquired, not inherited?
check.why: A scar comes from something that happened during life. Hair color, finger number and earlobe shape are inherited.

check.q: A flamingo stops eating pink shrimp and algae. What would you predict?
choices: Its feathers stay bright pink forever
check.why: The pink color comes from the food. Without it, new feathers grow in pale.

lessons.title: Traits That Help Find Food
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits give an individual an advantage in finding food, so that individual is more likely to survive and reproduce.
reading: Two great blue herons stand in a Chicago lagoon. One has slightly longer legs. It can wade into deeper water where more fish hide. It eats more. It stays stronger through the winter. A trait that helps a living thing survive is called an *advantage*. Long legs are an advantage for a heron. They would be no help to a mole.

Look at a bird's beak and you can often guess its food. A cardinal's thick beak cracks seeds. A woodpecker's chisel beak digs insects out of bark. A hummingbird's needle beak reaches nectar deep in flowers. Among woodpeckers, the ones with slightly stronger beaks may find more food in a hard winter.

Color can be an advantage too. A brown moth resting on brown bark is hard for a bird to see. This is *camouflage*, blending in. A white moth on the same bark stands out. The brown moth is more likely to live and have young. Its young are more likely to be brown. Over many generations, advantages like this add up.

words.d: a trait that helps a living thing survive or reproduce better than others of its kind
colors or patterns that help a living thing blend in with its surroundings

look.title: Winter at the Feeder
look.text: A backyard feeder in Peoria is filled with sunflower seeds. Cardinals crack the seeds easily with their thick beaks. A robin lands, pecks at a seed, and gives up. Robins have thin beaks made for pulling worms from soil. In January, the ground is frozen hard.
look.prompt: Which bird has the advantage at this feeder in January? What could happen to the robin?

check.q: Which beak is best for cracking hard seeds?
check.why: A thick, short beak, like a cardinal's, can squeeze hard enough to crack a seed.

check.q: A brown moth and a white moth rest on brown bark. Which is more likely to survive, and why?
choices: The white moth, because it is easier to see
The brown moth, because birds see it more easily
The brown moth, because it blends in and birds miss it
Both the same, because color does not matter
check.why: Camouflage hides the brown moth from birds. The white moth stands out and is more likely to be eaten.

check.q: Why do advantages 'add up' over many generations?
choices: Because the young of survivors often inherit the helpful trait
Because animals choose their traits each spring
Because all animals in a kind are identical
check.why: Survivors have young, and the young often inherit the trait. So each generation has more individuals with it.

lessons.title: Traits That Help Find a Mate
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits help an animal attract a mate, so that animal is more likely to reproduce and pass those traits on.
reading: A male cardinal in February is the reddest thing in a gray Illinois yard. That color costs him. Hawks can see him from far away. So why is he red? Female cardinals tend to choose brighter males to *mate* with. A bright male has more young. His sons tend to be bright too. The trait keeps going.

Sound works the same way. On a spring night, male frogs call from every pond. Each kind has its own call. Females move toward the loudest, clearest callers. On a summer night, male fireflies flash a code. A female that likes the pattern flashes back. Every song and flash is a way of saying, choose me.

The peacock's tail is the famous example. It is heavy and hard to hide. But peahens choose the males with the biggest, brightest tails. Darwin puzzled over this. A trait can be a burden for survival and still spread, if it helps an animal win a mate. Scientists call this *sexual selection*.

words.d: to pair up and reproduce; also, the partner an animal pairs with
when a trait spreads because it helps an animal attract a mate

look.title: The Feather That Made Darwin Sick
look.text: In an 1860 letter to a friend, Darwin joked that the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail made him feel sick whenever he looked at it. He could not yet explain how such a heavy, showy trait, which made the bird easier to catch, could exist. Later he argued that the tail spread because peahens preferred it.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, letter to Asa Gray, 1860 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why would a peacock's tail bother Darwin? What idea did he later use to explain it?

check.q: Why are male cardinals bright red even though hawks can see them?
choices: Females tend to choose brighter males, so bright males have more young
Red helps them hide in snow
check.why: Bright males win more mates and have more young, so the trait is passed on even though it has a cost.

check.q: How does a female firefly choose a mate?
check.why: Male fireflies flash a code. A female that likes the pattern flashes back.

check.q: A peacock's tail makes it slower to escape a fox. Why does the trait still spread?
choices: The tail also helps it fly faster
Peahens choose big-tailed males, so those males have more young
check.why: A trait can hurt survival and still spread if it helps win a mate. That is sexual selection.

lessons.title: Comparing Life Spans
lessons.mainIdea: Life cycles share the same stages, but the length of a life and of each stage varies enormously from one kind of living thing to another.
reading: How long is a life? For a monarch that hatches in June, about a month as a caterpillar and chrysalis, then a few weeks as an adult. For a monarch that hatches in late summer, much longer. That one flies to Mexico, rests all winter, and lives about eight months. Same kind of butterfly, very different *life span*.

Scientists measure life spans by tagging and counting. They put a tiny sticker, a *tag*, on a monarch's wing. They band birds' legs. They count *tree rings* in a stump; each ring is one year. A house mouse usually lives about two years. A dog, about twelve. A horse, close to thirty. A bur oak in an Illinois prairie can pass 300 years.

A long life is not always an advantage. A mouse lives a short life but can have several litters a year. An oak lives long but may not make acorns for twenty years. Each way of living has worked for a very long time. Comparing life cycles shows there is no single best way to be alive.

words.d: how long a living thing usually lives, from birth to death
a small marker put on an animal so scientists can track it
the layers of wood a tree adds each year, seen as rings in a cut trunk

look.title: Typical Life Spans
look.prompt: Which living thing on the list lives longest? About how many mouse lives fit in one dog life?

check.q: How can you tell the age of a cut tree?
choices: Count the rings in the trunk
check.why: A tree adds one ring of wood each year, so counting rings gives its age.

check.q: Using the data, about how many times longer does a horse live than a house mouse?
check.why: A horse lives about 28 years and a mouse about 2. 28 divided by 2 is 14.

check.q: A monarch that hatches in late summer lives much longer than one that hatches in June. What is the best explanation?
choices: The late-summer monarch migrates to Mexico and rests through the winter
It is a different kind of butterfly
June monarchs are eaten by birds
check.why: The late-summer generation flies south and rests all winter, living about eight months instead of a few weeks.

review.q: Which list shows the stages of a monarch's life cycle in order?
review.why: A monarch starts as an egg, hatches into a caterpillar, forms a chrysalis, and comes out as an adult.

review.q: A tadpole and an adult frog look very different. What is this change called?
review.why: Metamorphosis means a big change of body form as a young animal becomes an adult.

review.q: Which is the best example of an inherited trait?
choices: A bean plant that is pale from growing in a closet
A dog that is fat from too much food
A kitten with the same striped fur as its mother
A student who learned to speak Spanish
review.why: The kitten's stripes were passed from its mother. The others came from food, light or learning.

review.q: Two puppies in one litter have different colors. Why?
choices: Each got a different mix of traits from its two parents
review.why: Each puppy inherits traits from both parents, but the mix is different for each one. That is variation.
An acorn is the seed of an oak. When it germinates, it becomes an oak seedling.

review.q: A heron with longer legs can wade deeper and catch more fish. What is this trait an example of?
review.why: Longer legs help the heron get more food, so the trait is an advantage.

review.q: Male frogs call loudly on spring nights. What is the main purpose of the call?
review.why: Females move toward the loudest, clearest callers. The call helps a male win a mate.

review.q: A bean plant grown in a dark closet is tall, thin and pale. Its sibling in the sun is short and green. What caused the difference?
review.why: The plants came from the same pod. The difference in light, part of the environment, changed how they grew.

chapters.title: Structures, Senses and Survival
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the parts of a living thing help it stay alive, and what do fossils tell us about life that is gone?

story.title: The Fossil in the Mazon Creek Rock
story.kicker: A rust-colored lump from an old coal mine, a hammer tap, and a creature no one had ever seen.
paragraphs: South of Chicago, near the town of Braidwood, there are hills of gray and rust-colored rock. They are not natural hills. Machines piled them up when they dug for coal. Mixed into the piles are hard, rounded lumps called concretions. Most look like nothing. But some of them hold a secret. In 1955, a man named Francis Tully went walking there with a hammer.

Tully was a pipe fitter who hunted fossils on weekends. He picked up a lump and tapped it. It split along a hidden crack, like a book opening. Inside was the shape of an animal. It had a long, soft body, a thin neck ending in a claw with tiny teeth, and eyes on the ends of a stiff bar. Tully had never seen anything like it. Neither had anyone else.

He took it to the Field Museum in Chicago. The scientists were puzzled too. It was not a fish, not a worm, not a squid. They nicknamed it the Tully monster. In 1966, it got a scientific name: Tullimonstrum. Thousands more have been found since. Every one comes from this one small area in Illinois. In 1989, Illinois made it the state fossil.

The rock told a story too. About 300 million years ago, this part of Illinois sat near the equator. Rivers ran through a steamy swamp forest into a shallow sea. Ferns as tall as trees dropped their leaves in the mud. Jellyfish, shrimp, worms and Tully monsters lived in the water. When they died, mud buried them fast, and the mud slowly hardened into rock around them.

Today that swamp forest is an old coal mine, and part of the mine has filled with water. The ferns became coal. The mud became stone. The animals became fossils. Scientists still argue about what the Tully monster really was. But the fossil proves one thing for sure: the living things of Illinois, and the place itself, have changed almost beyond imagining.
story.think: The Tully monster's eyes sat on the ends of a stiff bar. What might that structure have been good for? How could you test your idea?

lessons.title: A Plant's Outside Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and thorns are external structures, and each one does a job that helps the plant survive, grow and reproduce.
reading: Pull a dandelion out of a sidewalk crack. Look at what comes up. A long, tough root went deep for water. A hollow stem held the leaves up toward light. Flat leaves caught sunlight to make food. A yellow flower made seeds. Each part is a *structure*, a part with a shape and a job.

Plants have parts for defense too. A rose has *thorns*, so deer think twice before biting. A cactus has spines and a thick waxy skin to keep water in. Some leaves are hairy or bitter. Milkweed leaks a sticky white sap that gums up the mouths of most insects. Monarch caterpillars are among the few that can handle it.

Structures help plants reproduce, too. Bright petals and sweet nectar bring bees. Bees carry *pollen* from flower to flower. A maple seed has a wing so it spins away from the parent tree. A burr has hooks that grab a passing dog's fur. Each structure solves a problem the plant cannot walk away from.

words.d: a part of a living thing that has a shape and a job
sharp points on a plant's stem that keep animals from eating it
a fine powder from flowers that must reach another flower for seeds to form

look.title: Two Plants in the Same Yard
look.text: A prairie plant called compass plant grows on the school prairie. Its root goes down about 3 meters, deeper than a basement. Next to it, a lawn grass has roots only a few centimeters deep. In August it has not rained for three weeks. The grass is brown and crunchy. The compass plant is still green.
look.prompt: Which root structure gave an advantage in the dry August? What might happen to each plant if the summer were wet instead?

check.q: What is the main job of a plant's roots?
choices: To take in water and hold the plant in place
check.why: Roots reach into the soil for water and anchor the plant. Leaves catch light, and flowers make seeds.

check.q: Why does a rose have thorns?
choices: To keep animals from eating it
check.why: Thorns are a defense structure. They make deer and other animals think twice before biting.

check.q: A maple seed has a thin wing. What problem does it solve?
choices: Getting the seed away from the parent tree
check.why: The wing makes the seed spin and drift, so it lands away from the parent and does not compete with it.

lessons.title: An Animal's Outside Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Shells, fur, feathers, claws, beaks and skin are external structures that protect animals and help them move, eat and stay warm.
reading: A painted turtle *basks* on a log in a Chicago lagoon. When a shadow passes, it slides into the water. Its shell is a bone box that a raccoon cannot bite through. Its *webbed* feet push it fast through water. Its eyes sit high on its head so it can see while nearly hidden. Every outside part has a job.

Animals that live through Illinois winters have parts for the cold. A white-tailed deer grows a thick, hollow-haired coat in fall. A chickadee fluffs its feathers to trap warm air. A frog cannot do either. It rests at the bottom of a pond and waits. Its skin is thin so it can take in oxygen from the water.

Parts for eating are easy to spot. A hawk has hooked *talons* to grab and a hooked beak to tear. A beaver has orange front teeth that never stop growing, so it can chew wood all its life. A mosquito has a needle mouth. Look at an animal's outside parts and you can often guess how it lives.

words.d: rests in the sun to warm up
having skin stretched between the toes, which helps push against water
the sharp, curved claws of a bird of prey such as a hawk

look.title: The Mystery Skull
look.text: A student finds a small skull in the woods near the Des Plaines River. It has long, sharp front teeth on top and bottom. The teeth at the back are pointed too, not flat. The eye holes face forward. The skull is about as long as your hand.
look.prompt: What might this animal have eaten? Which structures are your evidence?

check.q: What is a turtle's shell for?
choices: Protection from animals that would bite it
check.why: The shell is a bone box. A raccoon or other animal cannot bite through it.

check.q: Why do a beaver's front teeth keep growing?
choices: So it can chew wood its whole life without wearing them away
check.why: Chewing wood wears teeth down. Teeth that keep growing let the beaver keep chewing all its life.

check.q: A chickadee fluffs its feathers in January. What is it doing?
choices: Trapping warm air near its body
check.why: Fluffed feathers hold a layer of warm air against the skin, like a puffy coat.

lessons.title: Parts on the Inside
lessons.mainIdea: Internal structures, the heart, lungs, stomach, bones and brain, work together to keep an animal alive and growing.
reading: Press two fingers to the side of your neck. Feel the beat? That is your *heart*, a fist-sized pump. It pushes blood through tubes to every part of you. Blood carries oxygen and food to your body and carries waste away. A fish has a heart. So does a frog, a hawk and a mouse.

Take a deep breath. Your *lungs* filled with air. Oxygen from the air passes into your blood. A fish has no lungs. It pulls oxygen from water with its gills. Insects have no lungs either. They breathe through tiny holes along their sides. Different structures, same job: get oxygen in.

Your *skeleton* holds you up and guards what is soft. Ribs cage the heart and lungs. The skull is a helmet for the brain. A grasshopper wears its skeleton on the outside, like armor, and must shed it to grow. Your stomach breaks food into pieces small enough to use. Every inside part has a job, and the parts depend on each other.

words.d: the muscle that pumps blood through the body
the organs that take oxygen from the air into the blood
the bones that hold up a body and protect its soft parts

look.title: Resting Heartbeats Per Minute
look.prompt: What pattern do you see between an animal's size and its heart rate? How many times does a mouse heart beat while yours beats once?

check.q: What does the heart do?
check.why: The heart is a pump. It pushes blood, which carries oxygen and food, to every part of the body.

check.q: Fish have no lungs. How do they get oxygen?
choices: Through gills that pull oxygen from water
By coming up to breathe air every minute
check.why: Gills take oxygen out of water. Fish do the same job as lungs with a different structure.

check.q: Using the data, which is true?
choices: Bigger animals tend to have faster hearts
All animals have the same heart rate
Smaller animals tend to have faster hearts
check.why: The elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute and the mouse's about 550. Smaller animals have faster hearts.

lessons.title: How the Eye Uses Light
lessons.mainIdea: We see because light bounces off objects, enters the eye through the pupil, and forms an image that the eye sends to the brain.
reading: Turn off every light in a closet. You see nothing. Not because your eyes are broken, but because there is no light. Seeing needs light. Light from the sun or a lamp bounces, or *reflects*, off things. Some of that bounced light enters your eye. A red apple reflects red light to your eye. That is why it looks red.

Light enters through the *pupil*, the black hole in the middle of the eye. In dim light the pupil opens wide to let more light in. In bright sun it shrinks. Behind it sits a clear lens. The lens bends the light into a sharp, upside-down picture on the *retina* at the back of the eye. The retina is a screen packed with cells that react to light.

The retina changes light into signals. A thick nerve carries the signals to the brain. The brain turns the signals into what you see, and flips the picture right side up. Animals' eyes fit their lives. An owl's huge eyes gather dim light. A rabbit's eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it can watch for a fox almost all the way around.

words.d: bounces off; light reflects off objects and into our eyes
the dark opening in the middle of the eye that lets light in
the layer at the back of the eye that turns light into signals for the brain

look.title: Darwin Looks at the Eye
look.text: In 1859 Darwin wrote that it might seem absurd to think the eye, with its ways of adjusting focus, letting in different amounts of light and correcting for blur, could have formed step by step. But he added that if many small, useful steps could be shown, from a simple light-sensing spot up to a complex eye, the idea should not be called impossible.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859, chapter 6 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Darwin lists three things the eye can do. Which of them did you read about in this lesson?

check.q: Why can you not see in a completely dark closet?
choices: Your eyes shut down in the dark
There is no light to reflect off objects into your eyes
The retina only works in sunlight
The pupil closes all the way
check.why: Seeing needs light that bounces off objects and enters the eye. With no light, nothing reaches the retina.

check.q: What does the pupil do in dim light?
choices: Opens wider to let in more light
check.why: The pupil opens wide in dim light so more of the little light there is can get in.

check.q: A rabbit's eyes are on the sides of its head. What is the advantage?
choices: It can see almost all the way around for predators
It can see in total darkness
It can focus on tiny seeds
check.why: Side-facing eyes give a very wide view, so a rabbit can spot a fox coming from almost any direction.

lessons.title: Messages to the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Eyes, ears, skin, nose and tongue send information to the brain through nerves, and the brain uses it to decide what the body does next.
reading: A ball flies toward your face. Your hands come up before you have time to think. How? Your eyes sent a message to your brain along *nerves*, thin threads that carry signals. Your brain sent a message back down other nerves to your arm muscles. The whole trip took a fraction of a second.

Every *sense* works this way. Ears catch sound and turn it into signals. Skin has tiny *sensors* for touch, heat, cold and pain. The nose and tongue sense chemicals in air and food. All of the signals travel to the brain. The brain sorts them and decides. Loud bang? Jump. Smell of smoke? Look for fire. Hot pan? Let go.

Other animals lean on different senses. A dog's nose has far more smell sensors than yours. A bat sends out high squeaks and listens for the echoes to find moths in the dark. A catfish tastes with its whole skin. Each animal's senses fit how it gets food and stays safe. But a sense is only useful if its message reaches the brain.

words.d: thin threads in the body that carry signals to and from the brain
a way of taking in information: sight, hearing, touch, smell or taste
tiny parts that notice one kind of thing, such as heat or pressure, and send a signal

look.title: The Drum Bench Test
look.text: Two students sit at the site's drum bench. One wears a blindfold. The other taps a drum on the left, then the right, then far away. Every time, the blindfolded student points toward the sound, then says how loud it was. Then they try it with one ear covered. The pointing gets less accurate.
look.prompt: What information did the ears send to the brain? Why did covering one ear make pointing harder?

check.q: What carries messages from your eyes to your brain?
check.why: Nerves are thin threads that carry signals from the senses to the brain and from the brain to the muscles.

check.q: You smell smoke and go look for a fire. Put the steps in order.
choices: Brain decides, nose senses, body moves
Body moves, nose senses, brain decides
Nose senses, body moves, brain decides
Nose senses, brain decides, body moves
check.why: The sense comes first, the signal goes to the brain, the brain decides, and then the body acts.

check.q: How does a bat find a moth in the dark?
choices: By listening for echoes of its own squeaks
check.why: A bat sends out high squeaks and hears them bounce back off the moth. Its ears do the job eyes cannot in the dark.

lessons.title: The Brain Decides
lessons.mainIdea: The brain uses information from the senses, plus memory, to respond quickly and to learn from what happened before.
reading: A friend holds a ruler so it hangs just above your open fingers. Without warning, she drops it. You pinch. The ruler slides 15 centimeters before you catch it. That means it took about 0.17 seconds for your eyes to see it move, your brain to decide, and your fingers to close. That is your *reaction time*.

Try it ten times. Most people get a little faster. That is not because their nerves changed. It is because the brain learned. It stored a *memory* of the drop and got ready. Memory turns one experience into a better response next time. A squirrel that was chased by a hawk near the oak stays away from the oak.

The brain also decides what to ignore. Right now your skin feels your socks. Your brain is not bothering you about it. But if a spider crawled across your ankle, you would notice instantly. Sorting important signals from unimportant ones is one of the brain's biggest jobs. Animals that sort well tend to survive.

words.d: the time between noticing something and responding to it
information the brain stores from past experience

look.title: The Ruler Drop Test
look.cite: calculated from how falling objects speed up (free fall), rounded
look.prompt: A student catches the ruler at 20 cm the first try and at 10 cm the tenth try. What changed, and about how much time did she gain?

check.q: What is reaction time?
choices: The time between seeing something and responding to it
The time it takes to fall asleep
check.why: Reaction time is the gap between noticing something, like the ruler moving, and doing something about it.

check.q: Using the data, catching the ruler at 30 cm means a reaction time of about:
check.why: The table shows 30 cm matches about 0.25 seconds, a quarter of a second.

check.q: Why do people usually get faster after several tries of the ruler test?
choices: The brain remembers and gets ready
check.why: The brain stores a memory of the drop and prepares, so it responds a little sooner each time.

lessons.title: Living in a Group
lessons.mainIdea: Living in a group helps some animals get food, stay safe and raise young better than they could alone.
reading: In October, Canada geese fly over Chicago in a V. The goose in front breaks the air. The ones behind ride the smoother air and save energy. When the leader tires, another takes its place. Geese honk to keep in touch. A single goose would tire faster and have no one to watch for danger. The *flock* is a survival tool.

Wolves hunt in a *pack*. One wolf cannot bring down an elk. Six can. Prairie dogs live in towns with lookouts. When one spots a hawk, it barks, and everyone dives underground. Honeybees split the work. Some guard, some gather, some feed the young. Prairie dog towns and bee hives are kinds of *colonies*. A hive of thousands can do what no single bee could.

Groups have costs too. Food must be shared. Sickness spreads faster. So not every animal lives in a group. A bobcat hunts alone. Still, for many animals, the group means more eyes, more warmth and more help. Bison on an Illinois prairie stand shoulder to shoulder in a blizzard, sharing heat.

words.d: a group of birds that live or travel together
a group of animals, such as wolves, that hunt together
groups of animals of one kind that live together in one place, such as bees in a hive

look.title: Musk Oxen in a Ring
look.text: In the far north, a pack of wolves circles a herd of musk oxen. The oxen do not run. The adults turn to face outward and form a tight ring, horns out. The calves stand in the middle. The wolves pace, test, and finally leave. A lone musk ox, caught away from the herd, does not have this option.
look.prompt: How does the ring help the calves? What does the lone musk ox lose by being alone?

check.q: Why do geese fly in a V?
choices: Because the leader is the oldest
The birds behind save energy in the leader's smoother air
check.why: The front goose breaks the air, and the geese behind ride smoother air. They take turns leading.

check.q: What does a prairie dog lookout do?
choices: Warns the others when a predator comes
check.why: The lookout barks when it spots a hawk or coyote, and the whole town dives underground.

check.q: Which is a cost of living in a group?
check.why: Living close together means a sickness can pass quickly from one animal to the next. The others are benefits.

lessons.title: When the Pond Dries Up
lessons.mainIdea: When an environment changes, some living things survive in place, some move to a new place, and some die.
reading: A summer with almost no rain. By August, a pond near Springfield is a cracked mud flat. What happens to the living things? The answer is not the same for all of them. Some *survive* right there. Some move. Some die. Scientists watch which is which, and why.

Frogs with strong legs hop to a creek half a mile away. They move. Turtles dig into the damp mud below the surface and wait. They survive in place. Tadpoles cannot leave and cannot wait. They die. Cattail seeds sit in the dry mud, alive but not growing, ready for rain. The trait that matters is whichever one fits the new *conditions*.

Big changes have happened in Illinois before. Two hundred years ago, tall grass *prairie* covered most of the state. Then farms replaced almost all of it. Prairie chickens, which need wide grassland, nearly vanished. White-tailed deer, which like the edges of fields, are now everywhere. A change that hurts one kind can help another.

words.d: to stay alive through a hard time
the state of the environment: how wet, hot, cold or crowded a place is
a wide grassland with few trees; most of Illinois was prairie before farms

look.title: The Pond Count
look.text: A class counted living things at the pond in June and again in September, after the drought. June: 200 tadpoles, 30 frogs, 8 turtles, 50 dragonflies. September: 0 tadpoles, 3 frogs, 6 turtles, 2 dragonflies. A creek half a mile away had many more frogs in September than in June.
look.prompt: For each kind of animal, decide: did most survive in place, move, or die? What is your evidence?

check.q: The pond dries up. Which is the most likely outcome for a tadpole?
choices: It digs into mud and waits
check.why: A tadpole has no legs to leave and cannot wait in dry mud. Without water, it dies.

check.q: What are the three things that can happen to living things when the environment changes?
check.why: Some survive in place, some move to a new place, and some die. Which one depends on their traits.

check.q: Farms replaced Illinois prairie. Which sentence is true?
choices: Some kinds were harmed and some were helped
check.why: Prairie chickens nearly vanished, but white-tailed deer did well along the field edges.

lessons.title: How a Fossil Forms
lessons.mainIdea: A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually formed when it was buried quickly in mud or sand.
reading: Most dead things vanish. A fish dies in a river and other animals eat it. Bacteria finish the job. Even the bones crumble. But once in a while, a dead thing is buried quickly, by a flood of mud or a slide of sand. Under the mud, there is little oxygen. Rot slows to a crawl. This is how a *fossil* begins.

Over thousands of years, more layers pile on top. The mud is squeezed into rock. Water seeping through carries dissolved *minerals*. The minerals slowly replace the bone or shell, or fill the hollow it left behind. What remains is a copy in stone. Fossils can also be traces: a footprint, a burrow, a leaf print. These are *trace fossils*.

In 1669, a Danish doctor named Nicolas Steno made a simple claim. Rock layers form one on top of another, so the bottom layer is oldest. And the shark-tooth-shaped stones in the rocks were exactly that: sharks' teeth, turned to stone. Fossils were not strange rocks. They were once alive. Every fossil is a life that the earth kept a record of.

words.d: the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock
hard, nonliving materials in rock and water that can slowly replace bone or shell
fossils of something a living thing did, like a footprint or burrow, not of its body

look.title: Steno Reads the Layers
look.text: In 1669 Steno wrote that when a layer of sediment was being laid down, the layer beneath it must already have been solid, so lower layers are older than the layers above them. He also argued that objects found inside rock, such as shells and sharks' teeth, were placed there when the rock was still soft mud, and that they had once been the parts of living animals.
look.prompt: If you find a fish fossil in a layer below a fern fossil, which is older? How do you know?

check.q: Why does quick burial help form a fossil?
choices: Under mud there is little oxygen, so rot slows down
check.why: Buried under mud, the body is away from scavengers and oxygen, so it can last long enough to be replaced by minerals.

check.q: Which is a trace fossil?
check.why: A trace fossil records something an animal did, like walking. The others are parts of a body.

check.q: Steno said the bottom rock layer is usually the oldest. Why?
choices: Because layers form one on top of another over time
check.why: Each new layer settles on top of the last. So the deeper you go, the older the layer.

lessons.title: Inside the Mazon Creek Concretions
lessons.mainIdea: Mazon Creek fossils near Braidwood, Illinois, are unusually complete because soft-bodied animals were buried fast in mud that hardened around them.
reading: Most fossils are hard parts: bones, shells, teeth. Soft parts rot before they can be buried. That makes Mazon Creek special. Its rocks hold jellyfish, worms, shrimp, insects, and the Tully monster, soft bodies and all. Collectors find these *soft-bodied* animals inside rounded rust-colored lumps called *concretions*. Split one and it may open like a book.

Why here? About 300 million years ago, rivers poured mud into a shallow sea. Storms and floods buried animals and plants in minutes. Iron in the water hardened the mud around each body into a shell of stone before it could rot. The rest of the mud stayed soft and later washed away or became coal.

Coal mining brought the concretions to the surface. For years, collectors walked the *spoil piles* after rain, when wet rocks showed their cracks. Some soak the lumps in water and freeze them, over and over, until they split. Many of the best finds went to the Field Museum in Chicago. You can see a Tully monster there today.

words.d: having no bones or hard shell, like a jellyfish or a worm
hard, rounded lumps of rock that formed around something buried in mud
the heaps of rock and dirt a mine digs out and leaves behind

look.title: A Scientist Describes the Tully Monster
look.text: In 1966, Field Museum scientist Eugene Richardson described the new animal in the journal Science. He reported that it had a long body, a narrow front end like a neck that ended in a claw-shaped jaw with small teeth, and a stiff bar across the body with an eye at each end. He wrote that he could not place it in any known group of animals.
look.prompt: Richardson listed the parts he could see, but said he could not tell what group the animal belonged to. Why is it good science to say 'I do not know'?

check.q: Why are soft-bodied fossils so rare in most places?
choices: Soft animals never existed long ago
Soft parts rot before they can be buried
Soft animals live only in deserts
check.why: Soft bodies rot fast. Only quick burial and fast-hardening mud, as at Mazon Creek, can save them.

check.q: What is a concretion?
choices: A hard, rounded lump of rock that may hold a fossil
check.why: A concretion is a lump of rock that hardened around something buried in mud. Split open, it may show a fossil.

check.q: What happened to the Mazon Creek animals right after they died?
choices: They floated in the sea for years
Floods buried them in mud very quickly
check.why: Storms and floods buried them in minutes, and iron in the water hardened the mud before they could rot.

lessons.title: What Fossils Tell Us
lessons.mainIdea: By comparing fossils with living things and with the rocks around them, scientists learn what lived long ago and how the environment has changed.
reading: Illinois has no ocean. Yet *limestone* all over the state is packed with fossil sea creatures: corals, sea lilies, clam-like shells. Pick up a chunk of gravel and you may hold one. The only explanation is that a shallow sea once covered Illinois. The rocks are the evidence. Scientists *infer* the past from clues, the way a detective does.

Fossils also show what a place was like. Fern fossils from Mazon Creek match ferns that grow today only in hot, wet places. So Illinois was once hot and wet. Mammoth bones found in Illinois gravel pits show an ice-age world of cold grassland. Same ground, three different worlds: sea, swamp, ice.

Fossils show living things that are gone, too. No Tully monster swims anywhere today. No mammoth walks. Scientists say these kinds are *extinct*. Comparing an extinct animal's structures with living animals gives clues. A sharp, claw-like mouth means a hunter. Big eyes mean it found food by sight. Fossils let us ask questions about a world we can never visit.

words.d: a rock made mostly from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures
to figure out something you cannot see directly, using clues
no longer alive anywhere on Earth

look.title: Three Rocks From One Road Cut
look.text: Along a highway in central Illinois, a class studies a cliff of rock layers. Bottom layer: gray limestone full of fossil corals and shells. Middle layer: dark shale with fern prints and a thin seam of coal. Top layer: loose gravel and sand with no fossils, dropped by a glacier.
look.prompt: Put the three worlds in order from oldest to newest. What was Illinois like in each one?

check.q: Illinois has fossil corals but no ocean. What do scientists infer?
choices: A shallow sea once covered Illinois
Someone brought the fossils from Florida
check.why: Corals live in the sea. Finding them in Illinois rock means a sea was once here.

check.q: What does 'extinct' mean?
choices: No longer alive anywhere on Earth
check.why: An extinct kind of living thing has no living members left anywhere.

check.q: Fern fossils in Illinois match ferns that live in hot, wet places today. What can you infer?
choices: Illinois was once hot and wet
The ferns were planted by people
check.why: If the fossil ferns are like ferns that need hot, wet places, Illinois was probably hot and wet when they grew.

review.why: Lungs are inside the body. Thorns, fur and a shell are on the outside.

review.q: How does light let you see a red apple?
choices: The apple makes its own light
Light reflects off the apple into your eye
Your eye sends light to the apple
Red apples glow in the dark
review.why: Light from a lamp or the sun bounces off the apple. Some of it enters your eye and reaches the retina.

review.q: What is the job of nerves?
choices: To carry signals between the senses and the brain
review.why: Nerves are the threads that carry signals from the senses to the brain and from the brain to the muscles.

review.q: Which is a way living in a group helps wolves?
choices: Together they can catch prey too big for one wolf
They do not need to eat
review.why: One wolf cannot bring down an elk, but a pack can.

review.q: A forest burns down. What could happen to the animals that lived there?
choices: Some survive, some move, some die
review.why: When an environment changes, the outcome depends on each animal's traits: some survive in place, some move, some die.

review.q: Why are Mazon Creek fossils special?
choices: They are the oldest fossils on Earth
They show soft-bodied animals, which rarely become fossils
review.why: Fast burial and quick-hardening mud saved jellyfish, worms and the Tully monster, soft bodies and all.

review.q: Steno said rock layers form one on top of another. So a fossil in a lower layer is:
choices: The same age as one above it
review.why: Lower layers were laid down first, so a fossil in a lower layer is older.

review.q: A cactus has spines and a waxy skin. What problem do these structures solve?
choices: Keeping water in and animals away
review.why: The waxy skin holds water in, and the spines keep thirsty animals from biting.
